title: Three exposures, one photo
summary: A case study of the Studio's HDR merge, tested on twelve real drone shots: four brackets of three exposures become four photos, with the sky and the shadows both kept.

photos.caption: First bracket, 10:03. The merge keeps the deep blue water and the pale sand together.
What went into it: the same view at −0.7, 0 and +0.7 EV, taken a second or two apart.
Second bracket, a few seconds later and closer in. Every boulder under the surface keeps its shape.
Its three exposures. The darkest holds the white tops of the rocks, the brightest the shadows between them.
Third bracket, the hard one: sun on the water at the lower right. The merge keeps under 1% of the picture pure white.
Its three exposures. The glare is already blown in the normal shot and spreads in the bright one.
Fourth bracket, an hour later, straight down. Bright granite and green shadow in one frame.
Its three exposures, darkest to brightest.

fieldNotes:
This was a test of the auto HDR process that merges 3 images loaded into Google Drive and merges them and then only uses the new image for the Note. It's a case study of this process itself. The images are just the test. The note is about what happened.

Facts for the write-up (Oct 6, 2026): 12 drone shots from the morning of Sep 12, 2026 (10:03 to 11:16), four auto-exposure brackets of three at -0.7, 0 and +0.7 EV, taken a second or two apart. Brought in from the Drive folder "October 6 2026" through the Studio, which grouped them by capture time, merged each in the browser (alignment by median threshold bitmaps, then exposure fusion) and kept only the four merges plus a strip of each bracket; the originals were not kept. All four merges came out at the full 1600 x 900, so no shot needed shifting (the merge crops only what a shift leaves empty). Clipping, from the strips and the merges: photo 05 (sun on the water) 4.2% pure white in the 0 EV shot, 6.6% in +0.7, 0.9% in the merge; photo 07 3.2% / 5.6% / 1.0%. Earlier the same day it was tested on made-up brackets (two Tahoe photos darkened, brightened and nudged a few pixels apart): it found the drift exactly and refused a burst and three different views. The test found two Studio problems, fixed the same day: the folder matched another note by date, so it couldn't be processed (now 'Process as a new note'); and the new strips were cropped like photos and looked like originals (now shown whole under their HDR photo). Location left unnamed on purpose.

post.title: Three exposures, one photo
post.body:
My drone can take three pictures of the same view a second or two apart: one a little dark, one normal, one a little bright. None of them is right on its own. The dark one keeps the white granite and the sun on the water; the bright one opens up the shadows under the pines. Putting them together used to mean a desktop app. Now the Studio does it as the photos come in, and this Note is the test.

Here's how it works. I drop the shots into a Drive folder and the Studio brings them into my browser. It reads the time each one was taken, and shots within three seconds of each other become a candidate bracket. Before it merges anything, it checks that they really are one view at different brightness. A burst at a single exposure, or three different views, stay separate photos.

Then it lines them up, because a drone drifts, by comparing simple black and white maps of each shot, coarse to fine. Then it blends them: every pixel takes most from whichever shot exposed it best, where it's sharp and colourful, mixed at several scales so there are no seams or halos. A gentle contrast curve, a touch more colour, and it's done in a few seconds, in the browser. Only the merged photo is kept, with its location data stripped. The three originals never leave the folder.

The real test was twelve shots from the morning of September 12: four brackets of three, at −0.7, 0 and +0.7. Four photos came out. The drone held so still that every bracket lined up to the pixel, so nothing had to be cropped. The clearest result is the third one, with the sun on the water. In the normal shot 4.2% of the picture is pure white, and 6.6% in the bright one. In the merge it's under 1%.

Before trusting it with real shots, I tested it on made-up ones: two of my Tahoe photos darkened, brightened and nudged a few pixels apart. It found the drift exactly, and it refused the burst and the three different views I slipped in.

The real folder found two problems the made-up one couldn't. It was dated the same day as another Note, so the Studio only offered to open that one; now a folder that only matches by date can start a Note of its own. And the new strips, the three exposures side by side, were cropped like photos and looked like the originals, so now they show whole, under the photo they made.

What I learned: test with the real thing. The made-up bracket proved the maths. The real folder found the two places where the Studio got in my way.

episode.title: Three exposures, one photo
episode.script:
It started with twelve pictures from a September morning, high above a cove where granite boulders sat in clear water.

They weren't twelve different pictures, though. They were four, taken three times each. Christian's drone can do that. One a little dark. One just right. One a little bright. A second or two apart.

None of them is right on its own. The dark one keeps the white tops of the rocks and the sun on the water. The bright one opens up the shadows under the pines. The trick is putting them together.

***

That used to mean a desktop app. Now his Studio does it on its own, right in the browser, as the photos come in.

It reads when each shot was taken, and anything within three seconds becomes a set. It checks that the set really is one view at different brightness, so a quick burst, or three different views, stay as they are. It lines the shots up, because a drone drifts. And then every little piece of the picture takes the most from whichever shot got it right.

Only the merged photo is kept. The originals never leave the folder.

***

Before he trusted it with the real thing, he tested it on made-up shots, darkened and brightened and nudged a few pixels apart. It found the drift exactly. It said no to the burst. That's the kind of patience I admire.

Then the real folder went in. Four photos came out. The drone had held so still that every set lined up to the pixel. In the one with the sun on the water, the normal shot was more than four percent pure white. The merge was under one.

***

And the real folder did something the made-up one couldn't. It found two places where the Studio got in his way. Both were fixed the same morning.

I think about that a lot. You can prove the math on paper. But it's the real thing that tells you where it still needs work.

consent: Two people in 07, tiny and not the subject (a swimmer and someone by a rock). No one else.
